Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. We want to understand what you meant by "there was something near the bottom of the screen, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large dark "Continue Shopping" button positioned near the bottom of the screen, sitting prominently above the "Place Order" element — its label and placement in a checkout context felt unclear in purpose.

B) The "Place Order" button at the very bottom of the screen, which appears visually muted and lower in weight compared to the "Continue Shopping" button directly above it.

C) The small legal/disclaimer text block at the very bottom of the screen, beneath both buttons, referencing Terms of Service and Privacy Policy — present but easy to overlook given its position and size relative to the surrounding elements.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably B? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: When you look at both buttons side by side, what is it about how the "Place Order" button appears visually that makes it feel less important than "Continue Shopping"?
turns.a: I suppose it was the coloring. Everything on the page was in roughly the same... palette, I want to say. Nothing really contrasted with anything else. So my eye didn't go anywhere in particular. I'm not sure if that's intentional — maybe they wanted a calm, quiet look — but it made it harder to find the action.

turns.q: When you look at the page as a whole, which specific area or element stands out as the place where that sameness in palette is most noticeable to you?
turns.a: I kept looking at the lower part of the screen, I think. There was something there that didn't jump out the way I expected it to. Or maybe it was trying to and I wasn't reading it right. I'm not really sure.

turns.q: When you look at that lower part of the screen, what is it about how the "Place Order" button appears there that makes it not jump out the way you'd expect?
turns.a: I'm not entirely sure. Maybe because nothing on the screen was particularly telling me 'this is the action here.' It all looked sort of... equal weight. I've seen other apps where the main button is obvious right away. This one wasn't as obvious. I don't know if that's a problem or just my reading of it.

turns.q: What would the "Place Order" button need to look like on this screen for it to immediately read as the main action?
turns.a: I think because buttons need to tell you they're buttons. When you look at a screen, you're scanning for the thing you're supposed to do, and usually the most prominent thing is that thing. If the button is the same shade as the background, it stops looking like a button and starts looking like a label or a decorative element. You stop registering it as actionable.

turns.q: What would the "Place Order" button need to look like on this screen for it to immediately read as a button rather than a label?
turns.a: I think I'm saying the same thing in different ways. The coloring just makes everything look the same. I'm not sure what else to add.

turns.q: If you were looking at this screen and wanted to fix it, what specifically would you change about how the "Place Order" button looks so that it immediately stands apart from everything else?
turns.a: Because the whole point of that screen is to get someone to place an order. If the primary action that does that is nearly invisible — and I mean that somewhat literally, it was very pale text on a pale background, small font — then the screen is failing at its one job. It's not just friction. It's a broken affordance. You've designed an action that people can't see to take. The fix is direct: give the 'Place Order' button a solid fill color that contrasts with the background — not gray on gray — and make the text large enough to read at a glance. Something that immediately reads as 'this is what you press.' That's it. That's the root of it and the fix for it.
